entries.title: Palmer Luckey Made a Genetically Modified Military Dog Startup
entries.summary: Warhound came out of stealth on Wednesday with $200 million in funding and a mission to create “elite working dogs” equipped with "advanced body armor."
entries.content:
A new startup launched today with the definitely not terrifying mission of creating genetically enhanced dogs for the United States military, law enforcement, and emergency first responders.

Warhound is the brainchild of Anduril’s Palmer Luckey and Colossal Biosciences cofounder Ben Lamm. The startup has raised $200 million to “rebuild America’s domestic supply of elite working dogs” and reduce dependency on European dog breeders for military canines.

Lamm tells WIRED that Warhound is in the process of gene-editing its first batch of dogs. The startup has already collected blood samples from specific "top-performing” military, police, and first responder dogs in the United States, and its goal is to clone them. Breeds will be “mostly Belgian Malinois, some labs, and some shepherds,” he says. The company anticipates the first round of puppies to be born in early 2027.

The initial rounds of gene-editing will focus on eliminating common health conditions that impact these breeds, like hip dysplasia. Further down the line, Lamm envisions expanding to “really interesting things,” such as incorporating olfactory receptor genes from wolves to “enhance” the military dogs. (Colossal Biosciences is perhaps best known for its work on gene-edited wolves for its so-called Dire Wolf De-Extinction Project.)

Warhound, based in Texas, will also equip its canines with “Anduril’s advanced cybernetic Augments, software, and battlefield situational awareness,” according to a press release. Asked if this means the dogs will be some kind of cyborgs, Lamm clarifies that the plan right now is to supply them with tools like “advanced body armor” rather than, say, embedding some sort of computer in their dog bodies.

“So no dogs with lasers?” WIRED asked Lamm.

“I can’t comment on what Anduril plans,” he says. “Dog safety and performance, and then helping continue helping to improve the human handler and dog bond, and working as a team—that is what the mission is.”

Neither Luckey nor Lamm will be involved in Warhound’s day-to-day, although Lamm is on the company’s board, he says. David Spirk, a former Department of Defense chief data officer who most recently worked at Palantir, is serving as chief executive, and investors include In-Q-Tel, Sequoia Capital, and ARK Invest. Luckey is not an owner and does not have equity in the company, nor does Anduril; Colossal Biosciences does have an ownership stake.

Luckey and Lamm have been working on the project for over a year, Lamm says, and just recently decided to take the company out of stealth. “Someone said, ‘So it's like the Captain America dog program with the Ironman tech program on top of it,’” Lamm tells WIRED.

Everyone can agree that this is normal, and good, and that when the precision-designed beasts arrive on Earth, they will recognize that we are not the enemy.

The company plans to operate under the guidance of the American Humane Society.

entries.title: What to Know About Shamonda Virus Following the First Reported Human Infection
entries.summary: Although the case is considered exceptional, investigators are working to determine how the infection occurred and whether the pathogen played a role in the patient’s death.
entries.content:
France confirmed the death of the first person infected with the Shamonda virus, which is known to affect cattle, sheep, and goats and was previously considered non-transmissible to humans. The French government asserts that, based on current knowledge of this pathogen, there is no risk to the general public. It emphasized, however, that health authorities are continuing to investigate.

The report specifies that the case occurred in Lyon. The patient, who died earlier this month, suffered from severe immunosuppression, making this likely an exceptional case. “The neurological complications observed in the immunocompromised patient prior to his death were most likely related to infection with the Shamonda virus,” the official statement notes.

According to preliminary evidence, the patient contracted Shamonda virus from an insect bite. A tiny gnat known as the biting midge is known to be the primary route of transfer between animals. Since the virus was first identified in Nigeria in the mid-1960s, sporadic infections have been reported in livestock across Africa as well as in Japan. Cattle are considered the primary host because they develop visible symptoms. (Although sheep and goats can become infected, no obvious clinical signs have been documented in these animals.)

After animal is bitten by a midge carrying Shamonda virus, the infection has an incubation period of two to three days. Symptoms observed in animals include fever, diarrhea, and a decrease in milk production. When pregnant cows have become infected, the virus can cause miscarriages or severe deformations in the calf.

To date, there is no vaccine, so prevention and control measures rely on the use of insecticides and repellents. That doesn’t mean you should panic. Public health authorities are considering the case to be “exceptional,” because the deceased patient was severely immunocompromised.

Still, several European countries are on alert, because until a few months ago, this region was considered free of the virus. However, this summer, a new variant known as Shamonda-Europe was detected in livestock in Switzerland. Other cases were subsequently identified in Germany, France, Austria, Belgium, the Netherlands, Liechtenstein, Italy, and Spain.

Spain’s Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries, and Food states that two genetically distinct forms of the virus, known as Shamonda Type 1 and Shamonda Type 2, have been identified circulating in Europe. It adds that, in early September, infections of both types were confirmed on livestock farms in 37 provinces across France.

The case documented in France constitutes the first known infection in a person.

X content

“This is an important scientific finding. However, it is important to put this into perspective. The patient had a serious underlying illness that left them particularly vulnerable to infections, and we do not yet know whether Shamonda virus contributed to their death,” Ben Brennan, professor of virology at the University of Glasgow, said in a statement.

It’s premature to draw conclusions about the virus and it’s potential to infect humans, agreed David Roiz, a scientist Institute for Game and Wildlife Research in Spain. Many viruses “circulate naturally amongst mammals in tropical regions and cause sporadic cases in humans,” he said. “In a globalized world, where animals and goods are on the move and the climate is changing, it is not unusual for cases of human transmission to occur, and we should not be concerned; we simply need to monitor the situation, remain vigilant, and be proactive in addressing potential health risks.”

This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

entries.title: The Google Home Speaker Has Been Secretly Eating My Wi-Fi Data
entries.summary: My Google Home Speaker had been burning through more data than all the rest of my devices combined. As I looked into it further, I found other smart home devices that had the same problem.
entries.content:
If you had to estimate how much data your smart speaker was using over the course of a couple of weeks, would you guess 3 terabytes? That's what one Google Home Speaker user discovered when he checked his home Wi-Fi's usage, according to Reddit posts reported on by 9to5Google. The Google Gemini–powered smart speakers have apparently been downloading huge amounts of data to the device over the past two weeks, which could put a serious damper on your Wi-Fi network.

While it isn't happening to everyone, after checking my own home internet usage, I found out that I have been experiencing the same issue. My Google Home Speaker has used 487 GB of data in the past 10 days, using almost as much as the entire rest of my home between August and September.

Google confirmed this bug has only affected some devices and that it has rolled out a solution. A spokesperson from Google told WIRED: “A server misconfiguration caused some Google Home Speakers to repeatedly download a software update. This issue has now been resolved.”

Looking into this issue made me go beyond just Google's usage, though. My husband and I started reviewing the data usage for all of the individual devices that our router could identify and found some surprising numbers. The weirdest highlight was that Amazon was listed as using 22 GB in the past week with only the Ring smoke detector set up in my house, which was similar to the use of one of the smartphones in my house. There's also a mysterious device just labeled “WATCH” that used about 21 GB in the past week, but no one in my home has a smart watch that's been on in the last year. A mystery for me to solve another day.

If you've noticed your home Wi-Fi bandwidth isn't what it used to be, it could be because one of your smart home devices (or possibly something else entirely). Here's how to check your router or Wi-Fi provider for which device could be at fault.

How to Check Your Device Usage

You have a couple of options for checking how much data a smart home device has been using. Some routers provide detailed information about where all your data is going, for starters. I have an Eero mesh system for my house, but we don't pay for its subscription fee to access detailed information—so it's fairly limited. The free version of the app lists all the connected devices in my home, but it doesn't tell me how much data each uses.

There are a lot of routers that have subscription fees and paywalls that can hide this information and other features you might want. But our favorite subscription-free mesh Wi-Fi system comes from Asus, which also makes our favorite regular Wi-Fi router, and you can track and analyze traffic for free with an Asus router. Here's how:

  • Open the web interface (go to http://www.asusrouter.com/ in your browser) and log in.
  • Click on the Traffic Analyzer tab and make sure it's turned on (data is refreshed every hour).
  • You can see the top five clients using data listed on the Statistic tab.
  • You can also see live traffic in the Asus Router app on your phone.

Folks with a TP-Link router or mesh can also review traffic. Here's how:

  • Open the Deco or Tether app.
  • Tap on the Network tab and select Traffic Usage.
  • What you see will depend on the model you have, but with some routers you can toggle on In-depth Statistics for more detailed information.

Netgear only tracks overall traffic under Traffic Meter, you can't break it down by device. For other manufacturers it's worth poking around in the web interface. (It usually gives you access to more data than the mobile app.) If you're looking to get more information without hitting a paywall, explore both our router and mesh Wi-Fi guides for recommendations.

But there's another way. I used our internet provider's app to check exact usage data. Mine is the AT&T app, but most internet providers should have an app or login you can use to check your data activity. My data appears right at the front of the app underneath my current usage. It's more limited than the info you'd get from a dedicated router's app if you did subscribe; I'm only able to view detailed data by today, the past seven days, my current AT&T billing period, or over the past three billing periods. And the app only lists a handful of high-volume devices versus every device connected to the internet in my home.

But even that limited information revealed which devices were gobbling up the most data in the recent days and weeks, which is how we discovered the issue with both the Google Home Speaker and the Ring smoke detector.

Why Should You Check?

It's not a huge issue for me that my Google Home Speaker has been guzzling my data. I have a large Wi-Fi plan (a must as a smart home tester), and it was patched quickly. On the other hand, I have unplugged it for the time being to make sure I don't hit the 2 terabyte cap we have per billing period. But if you're on a plan where massive downloads like this can cost you, or your signal is getting clogged up by mysterious devices, it might be time to check your data usage to find out which device is at fault. You never know when you'll find a 3-terabyte bug slowing your whole network.

entries.title: The Social Society Helping Women Join the AI Boom
entries.summary: WIRED spoke with the founders of the Aged Intelligence Society, a fast-growing events startup that brings women together to “solve midlife problems using frontier tools.”
entries.content:
I’m not even going to try to pretend I don’t have a bit of a girl-crush on Shoshana Berger. She’s a former WIRED editor turned editorial leader for companies like Notion and Ideo. She’s super smart and chic. And she’s the cofounder, with Nina Willdorf, of the Aged Intelligence Society, a buzzy events startup that hosts invite-only dinner parties where women “solve midlife problems using frontier tools.”

Berger and Willdorf having a refreshingly practical take on AI. “This is the most formative technology of our generation, and it’s here,” Willdorf says. “If you choose to sit it out, you are doing yourself a disservice.”

That thesis resonates. Their events have been oversubscribed since day one. The second dinner party they hosted was covered by The New York Times. Hundreds of women reached out asking to attend future events. Their Substack, where they share tools and tips, quickly got over 1,000 subscribers, including a New Yorker writer and a small-town mayor. Women outside the Bay Area are now hosting their own Aged Intelligence meetups.

They also practice what they preach, especially as they juggle kids entering college, their own aging parents, and their increasingly in-demand business. “The midlife cognitive and emotional labor is so heavy and so intense that we need an assistant,” Berger says. “Actually, we need the National Guard, but AI will help in the interim.”

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

Zoë Schiffer: How did the Aged Intelligence Society start?

Shoshana Berger: Nina and I are both recovering magazine editors. We ended up at a friend's birthday party, and we were both obsessing over Claude, our new French lover. All the other women had glazed eyes while we were talking; they just weren’t part of the conversation. At some point I said, “Nina, I think this might be a business, because all these women need to be doing what we're doing.”

Nina Willdorf: We were super nervous before the first event …

Berger: We needed to take beta blockers and ashwagandha because we were like, wait, we're inviting all of these baller women, these really smart, incredibly accomplished women, and we’re not AI experts. But we have been doing what we usually did as reporters, which is test the tools in a way many women did not seem to be doing.

There's a million reasons for women to bow out of the conversation, and we were like, “no, no, no, you cannot bow out of this conversation if you are going to be relevant in the work world. You need to be fluent.”

Willdorf: We are not like pom-pom advocates for everything about this, but we feel committed to this idea that being involved is really important.

How do you set up expectations around the event for attendees?

Berger: There are rules of engagement for every party. One is we have an ideological parking lot. So if you want to talk about how AI is going to ruin everything, this is not the best space to do that. There are lots of ways in which we are also terrified about AI and find it can be quite menacing, especially for creatives like us, but that's not what we're here to do. We're here to gain fluency, test things out, and reduce our administrative load.

Willdorf: And eat some really good cheese and drink some wine.

Berger: We have everyone bring a laptop and a midlife problem. We call it a midlife quandary. We spend 15 minutes doing what we call library time. We all bring our laptops out, and you work on your problem. And Nina and I kind of walk around the room sherpa-ing people through the experience: “You might want to try this tool, try this LLM instead. Your prompt is feeling a little weak. You're not getting the answer that you like. Let's work on that and iterate.”

Willdorf: Sometimes people are like, “You know what? I don't really want AI to write for me.” And we're like, “Oh no, no, we don't either. Let us show you a couple other things you can think about.”

You’ve had a wait list for these parties since you started. How do you decide who gets to attend?

Willdorf: We have really found that the optimal number is between like eight and 12. When it gets bigger than that, it's a little bit chaotic. Our best events have been ones where there is a magical mix, and you have somebody that works in nonprofit next to somebody who works in design next to somebody who is home with the kids next to a CEO next to someone who works in philanthropy.

Most people, in my experience, cannot immediately identify a software-shaped problem in their life. How do you help people see an issue that AI could actually help with?

Berger: So much of what we're trying to do is show the pragmatic ways in which it's helping with midlife overload. We're often labeled the sandwich generation. We hate that term because it just sounds like we're the tasteless tomato in between two slabs of bread. But the real part of that is that we are dealing with parents who increasingly need help and kids who maybe are launching, maybe not.

One woman came to an event with a mother who was dealing with an Alzheimer's diagnosis, and she wanted to know whether her mother was qualified for long-term care because she had an insurance plan. Well, the insurance carrier sent her a 300-page packet. Who is going to read through that? This is how insurance companies keep you from using your insurance policy. So of course, she fed it to AI. And the AI came back saying, yes, your mother is absolutely qualified for care, and would you like me to write a letter to the insurance company to argue your case?

When I first started out as a consultant, I, in a typical female way, completely lowballed my consulting fee. I fed my proposal to Claude and said, “What's wrong with this? Make this bulletproof.” And it came back and said, “You're not charging enough for this scope of work.” And I was like, “Well, what should I charge?” And it said, “Start by doubling your rate.” I took a deep breath, and I did it. The client did not blink.

I feel that a lot of people don’t want to get near AI because they see slop and get the ick. But you’re talking about something different—using AI for economically valuable tasks.

Berger: The economic value piece is really important, because women have long suffered from being stuck at home as domestic laborers, because we weren't seen as economically valuable in the marketplace, right? So the idea behind Aged Intelligence Society is that if anyone needs to optimize their time, it's women.

In some ways, AI is the new washing machine or the new laundry or whatever it is. It's giving women many, many hours of the day back by offering them automation.

The reason we narrowed the aperture to people 40-plus is that we feel like the product-market fit for women who are over 40 is so spot on. One, because we have very discerning taste after many decades of honing it. We know how to ask really sharp questions. We have very strong bullshit meters, so we're not going to take just the first answer. We're going to keep probing and pushing.

And so we feel like in some ways this tool was built for people who have a certain level of intelligence and accrued experience. It's not really built for young people. It's not built for people who have not already gone through the failure and the friction of life and learned for themselves what makes for a good question.

entries.title: Inside the Exclusive Nathan Fielder Interview
entries.summary: This week on “Uncanny Valley,” we go behind the scenes of our Nathan Fielder cover story, unpack tech billionaires’ generous promises, and discuss the suspicious letters sent to US election offices.
entries.content:
This week, Brian Barrett and Leah Feiger speak with WIRED global editorial director Katie Drummond to go behind the scenes of her viral interview with Nathan Fielder about his latest documentary, You Can See Everything. She tells us why she had to keep it a secret—and how it felt to interview a man who hates being interviewed. We also discuss why tech billionaires are feeling generous all of a sudden, from Anthropic’s pledge to commit 5 percent of its shares to a public benefit fund to Elon Musk’s promise to give a SpaceX share to every child in America. Plus, a WIRED investigation found that election offices in at least 32 states received suspicious letters, some containing white powder, just two weeks before the midterms.

You can follow Brian Barrett on Bluesky at @brbarrett, Katie Drummond on Bluesky at @katie-drummond, and Leah Feiger on Bluesky at @leahfeiger. Write to us at [email protected].

Articles mentioned in this episode:

  • Nathan Fielder Tells Us Everything
  • How Elizabeth Holmes Tricked WIRED—and Everyone Else
  • Election Offices in at Least 32 States Have Received Suspicious Letters
  • They Fled Trump’s America. Now They Regret It

How to Listen

You can always listen to this week's podcast through the audio player on this page, but if you want to subscribe for free to get every episode, here's how:

If you're on an iPhone or iPad, open the app called Podcasts, or just tap this link. You can also download an app like Overcast or Pocket Casts and search for “Uncanny Valley.” We’re on Spotify too.

Transcript

Note: This is an automated transcript, which may contain errors.

Brian Barrett: Well, welcome to WIRED's Uncanny Valley. I'm Brian Barrett, executive editor.

Leah Feiger: And I'm Leah Feiger, director of politics and science. This week, we're diving into the behind-the-scenes of our interview with Nathan Fielder. WIRED's global editorial director, Katie Drummond, was among a small group of people who saw Fielder's latest documentary, You Can See Everything, way before its release. She spoke with Fielder at length and will be joining us to share what stayed with her after their interview.

Brian Barrett: We'll also get into Anthropic and Elon Musk pledging to share their riches with the public. Anthropic announced that it would commit 5 percent of company shares to a public benefit fund, and Musk followed suit by promising he would give one SpaceX share to every child in America. We'll discuss the motivations behind these pledges and the chances that they'll actually happen.

Leah Feiger: And we're also going to take a look at the harassment campaign that has hit election offices across the country just two weeks before the midterms. A WIRED investigation found that election offices in at least 32 states have received suspicious letters, some of them containing white powder. We'll talk through what happened and how election officials are responding.

Brian Barrett: If you've been online this past week, chances are you've heard about Nathan Fielder and codirector Lance Oppenheim's latest documentary, You Can See Everything. The documentary follows Fielder—a graduate of Canada's top business schools, fun fact—as he spends a month inside Elizabeth Holmes' home in the weeks before she went to prison. Holmes was convicted back in 2022 for defrauding investors with Theranos, her blood testing startup. Turns out the speedy and accurate blood tests were fake. Innovative tech didn't actually exist. More importantly, though, the film was kept secret for three years. Only a few dozen people saw it before it debuted at the Telluride Film Festival. One of those people was WIRED's global editorial director, Katie Drummond. She had signed an NDA to hear what the film was about, got Nathan Fielder to be on WIRED's cover, and sat down with him for almost an hour and a half. Katie, thank you for joining us.

Katie Drummond: What a wonderful introduction. You made me sound so special. Thank you, Brian. I'm so happy to be here.

Brian Barrett: Yeah, I'm also excited, genuinely, because this is, I think, our first Uncanny Valley crossover episode?

Katie Drummond: It is.

Leah Feiger: Katie, what were your first thoughts when Fielder's publicist reached out? Tell us everything.

Katie Drummond: I'll tell you. You can hear everything. I was on my way to dinner with a very good friend, and I was in an Uber, and I got an email from him that said, "Do you have a few minutes to talk about Nathan Fielder?" And if you know me at all and my taste in comedy and the kind of TV I watch, you would know that I have many minutes to talk about Nathan Fielder and I would talk about Nathan Fielder anytime. I'm genuinely a big fan. I think his stuff is so, so brilliant and so clever and … I don't want to say “genius” because I just think that's a step too far, but I think it's very, very good. I'm a big fan. So I wrote back and said, "I have all the time in the world." And we talked that night, and he just said, "Nathan has this project coming out. Only a few dozen people know what it is. And I can't tell you anything else about it until you agree to sign an NDA, but would you be interested in him for a cover, and do you have a cover that you could put him on this fall?" And to be honest, I had no idea if we had a cover that we could put him on this fall. I couldn't even remember if we had another print issue coming out this year. But I was just like, "Yes, of course. We totally have a cover." I lied and then immediately texted Reyhan, who runs the print magazine, and was like, "Do we have a cover available this fall?" And then it turned out that we did, and I signed an NDA, and she signed an NDA as well. And only after we signed the NDAs did they even say it's a movie. I thought it could have been anything. That's how little they were willing to share with us until we agreed not to talk about it.

Leah Feiger: Were you hesitant at all? Could this have been a bit?

Katie Drummond: There were times when I was sort of like, "Are we somehow being incorporated into the joke?" When they did The Rehearsal season 2 … I don't know if listeners have seen it. If you haven't, you should. I think it's incredible. But Nathan did this CNN appearance with Wolf Blitzer …

Wolf Blitzer, archival audio: Here with us now, comedian, 737 pilot, and host of The Rehearsal, Nathan Fielder.

Katie Drummond: … where he very seriously talked about aviation safety in a way that I think CNN was happy with, but if I, in my role running WIRED, if that happened to me, I don't know that I would be happy about being part of the joke. So I definitely worried about that. But once we saw the movie and talked to them more about what they wanted to do, it was pretty clear that this was just a good faith, earnest attempt to get Nathan to do some press, which he does not often do.

Brian Barrett: It wasn't a bit, turned out to be a real interview, but one thing I thought was really interesting about it was he turned the tables on you at some point. It felt like he started trying to interview you. What was that like in the moment, and were you … You sort of catch yourself. It's sort of a fun moment, I think, in the interview. You say, "Wait a minute, you derailed me. That was rude." What was it like actually trying to interview someone who was so used to being on the other end of it?

Katie Drummond: It was a tough interview. He was very pleasant. He was totally lovely, and it was a very good-faith conversation. But he doesn't like being interviewed. I mean, he says that in the interview. He says, "I hate this. I hate that this is happening to me right now."

Brian Barrett: Relatable.

Katie Drummond: Yes. I think he genuinely doesn't feel very comfortable expressing himself with words. I think he has talked before in interviews about how that is a real weakness for him, and so I think he feels uncomfortable trying to do it. And I think he did not want to share his feelings about what he experienced making the film, because he didn't want that to inform the opinion of someone going in to see the movie. If they think like, "Well, Nathan thought this about Elizabeth and he thought this about Elizabeth's partner and he thought this and this about Theranos," he didn't want that to color how people saw the movie, and so he felt much more comfortable asking me questions about what I thought about the movie. And I think genuinely he is still trying to figure out what happened to him in the three years that he was making it, and asking people what they thought is helpful for him.

Leah Feiger: And I suppose this is a good time to say for all of our listeners that if you haven't seen the film yet, there's no spoilers in this interview. Both of you did a really good job of skating around that. But you did talk about seeing the film twice and having different reactions each time. Your conversation with him, as spoiler-free as it was, as difficult as it was to keep him on track, to get him to share his own viewpoints here, did it change at all how you saw the film?

Katie Drummond: Oh, that's interesting. The conversation and then reading the interview back, which I had to do many times as we edited it and got it ready to publish it, and then looking at the questions I asked him and thinking about why I asked certain questions in the moment did make me reflect on the movie more. There was one thing I said to him in the interview where I said, "We don't really know, Nathan, what you are thinking in the film and how you feel about these people." And then I thought more about that afterward and disagreed with myself in the end, where I'm like, no, it actually is pretty clear in his facial expressions or how he talks to people, or even knowing that he was a codirector on the film. So he made decisions about what they included and what they didn't include and how they frame and set up certain subjects. So obviously with all of those things combined, we do get a sense of what his point of view is. You can tell what the filmmaker's point of view is to some extent as you're watching the movie. So it did make me think a lot about the film. I mean, I will say I have thought way too much about this movie just because I've been getting ready for this interview, doing the interview, editing the interview, getting ready to publish it. I am ready to stop thinking about it. I would like that to happen.

Leah Feiger: This is your life now.

Katie Drummond: I hope not.

Brian Barrett: I was going to say, but Katie, the interview's gotten a lot of attention since it published. You've gotten a lot of attention since it published for the interview. What's it been like? I think as journalists, the adage is you don't want to become the story, not that you've become the story here, but I feel like there's been a lot of demands on your time. You've been on TBPN, a lifelong goal of yours. You're on Uncanny Valley, another lifelong goal. What has it been like processing being wrapped up in this sort of engine of attention that the documentary's been getting?

Katie Drummond: I pivoted from being a reporter to being an editor for exactly this reason, which is that I really didn't like getting attention on the internet. I found it very unpleasant. I continue to find it unpleasant. So in that regard, I don't like it. I like to talk to commenters and sort of respond to good-faith things, but then you also, it's 8:30 at night and you're on Reddit and you read a thread, and people are like, "This is some of the worst writing I've ever seen," and you're like, "Oh, wow, OK. That person doesn't like me," and that's hard. I think I just want to hopefully genuinely encourage people to see the movie. And I don't mean that because I'm being paid to do an advertisement for them; I'm certainly not. It's just a really interesting project. And so I'm just really proud that we were able to play a teeny tiny part in it. If I could clear up one thing that has generated some public attention since the interview came out is that my Google search results now lean heavily toward Katie Drummond felon, Katie Drummond criminal, Katie Drummond conviction. I just want to be very clear, it can be hard to read tone in writing sometimes, that was a joke.

Brian Barrett: But in the eyes of AI overviews, you are forever a felon.

Katie Drummond: And that's how this movie ruined my career. Yeah. Yep.

Leah Feiger: That's really the subject line. Not only did you release this interview, WIRED released a slate of stories related to Nathan Fielder. And in one piece, former WIRED editor, Adam Rogers, discusses how the magazine was one of the first outlets back in the early 2010s to praise Theranos, to give them all of this public attention. So there's this real reckoning that happens in that story. I'm really curious, I would love to hear from you about the decisions that went into even publicizing this mistake and this clearly new, this division between old era and new era.

Katie Drummond: Yeah. When I read Adam's story, I read a draft of it last week, I was so blown away. I mean, if anyone listening hasn't read it, it's such a great piece of writing, and it's such a sharp reckoning with the editorial decisions that were made around that interview. I would just say, I think that that piece and this film say a lot about where WIRED is in this moment. And there were so many really smart people who worked at WIRED in that era. It's not like this was a bunch of dumb people making dumb decisions. It was really smart people making really smart decisions. But they existed and WIRED operated in this context where even in sort of the early 2010s, as a lot of controversy was starting to emerge around these tech companies and the rise of social media and the ills that came with that, there was still much more a culture of celebrating and lionizing startup founders and really wild emerging ideas, maybe not giving them the scrutiny that they ought to have had. I think Liz Holmes played into that really effectively. I think that her relative youth and her gender were important factors there, that the media loved the idea of a young woman becoming this self-made billionaire with this incredible innovation in personalized medicine. I think that the journalist who did that interview in 2014 asked Liz hard questions. Didn't necessarily get satisfying answers, but I think that, as Adam points out, the WIRED of today would've asked much tougher questions or would've even had a much higher bar to cover Theranos to begin with. I don't know that we necessarily would've looked at this startup that hadn't actually made many inroads into commercializing their product and said, "Yeah, that feels like something we should do a straight interview on." I don't know that we would've even made that decision. So I just think, again, it was really smart people making smart decisions within the context that they were operating at the time, but I think that context has really changed. And I think there's a lot more necessary skepticism of these people and their ideas and where this money is coming from and how and why they're getting that money to begin with and what they're doing with it.

Brian Barrett: Katie, thank you so much for being here.

Katie Drummond: Thank you guys.

Brian Barrett: Shifting gears to current tech companies, some of them have been on a philanthropic streak of sorts. On Sunday, Anthropic said it would commit 5 percent of its shares to a public benefit fund meant to address AI's impact on the labor market. A day later, Elon Musk, not wanting to be left out apparently, posted on X that next year he's going to give one SpaceX share to every kid in America, and that this will be the first of many. Both announcements don't contain much detail on how this will actually happen, you'll be shocked to hear. According to Anthropic's statement, though, the fund could make charitable donations or direct money to "specific populations." We love a specific population. Musk gave no further details for his plan, but that didn't stop President Trump from publicly thanking him. Leah, are you excited for all the shares in AI companies that you and future generations of America are going to get?

Leah Feiger: I can't wait, Brian. I mean, I've just been bated breath for this to happen. I have so many thoughts about this, and I'm sure that you do as well. The idea of tech companies using wealth for public good has been an ongoing conversation for literal decades, and it's stalled in recent years. It just 100 percent has. Elon Musk, the richest man in the world, famously is anti-philanthropy, which is very new, to be clear, from tech of even a decade ago, that at the very least you had the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation, you had an outpouring of support for the climate corners of the tech industry and dumping money into that. That's all dried up, and I'm not honestly sure that we've spent enough time talking about that. A lot of these companies have kind of relied on the positive press from their forebears literally 15 years ago. And so the idea that there's now this whole philanthropic streak of, as you said, sorts is of note. It's the idea that like, oh, OK, we're actually that unpopular that we need to weigh in to some respect. We're going to take your jobs, but we're going to now fund the specific populations, question mark, whose jobs were taken? I have so many questions here.

Brian Barrett: No, that's the thing. And I think we can sort of disambiguate the Musk thing from the Anthropic thing because the Musk thing, A, Elon Musk makes so many promises, and who knows—

Leah Feiger: Oh my god, yeah. That doesn't even count to me. The fact that people were sharing it credulously ... I'm sorry, Natasha Lyonne, get a grip. This is clearly not occurring.

Brian Barrett: And even if he does, it is a lot of money, in fairness. It's $10 billion or so based on the current stock price. But it's 0.5 percent of overall SpaceX stock—

Leah Feiger: And it's not happening. It's just not happening.

Brian Barrett: Yeah. And even if it did, it would be 150 bucks in everybody's account, which is not going to make anybody rich. It's fine. So set that aside for a moment. But let's talk about Anthropic, because I do think, to your point, it's philanthropy, but it's philanthropy born of this sense that we're going to make all the jobs go away, so … It is really, we're going to sort of start making some inroads toward universal basic income. But it's UBI as dictated by Anthropic. It's the sense of, "We're going to be the ones to figure out not only how AI is going to reshape society, but we're going to be the ones responsible for then making sure everybody's OK." The amount of power that they're trying to invest in themselves is really astonishing.

Leah Feiger: We live in an unregulated hellhole. Put it on a T-shirt. Look, Anthropic is preparing for a trillion-dollar IPO right now. And I know, it's me, so I have to say it, the midterms are in two weeks. All anyone is talking about in at least a portion of these polls is data centers, how unpopular they are, how unpopular AI is. The use of AI is a bipartisan issue at this point, which is fascinating. We should really be talking about how impressive it is that these massive companies have made so many people hate them so quickly. So it's all this timing, all of these, "Don't look at the man behind the curtain," facade that I just can't get over.

Brian Barrett: One thing that's kind of fun here … I can't take credit for this observation. This was Matt Levine in Money Stuff in Bloomberg. But he made this point that I think is really apt, which is that the ways in which this money is being proposed to be distributed really reflects each company's or individual's sense of self. So you've got Anthropic, as we talked about, "Only we have the power. We're the only ones responsible enough to do this." You've got Elon Musk, very individual entrepreneurship, "We're going to give everybody a little stock and see where it goes." And then you also had … We haven't confirmed this independently, but OpenAI reportedly in July, according to the Financial Times, proposed or considered giving the US government a 5 percent stake, which is sort of OpenAI saying, "Hey, we'll play ball. We'll work with the government. We'll figure this out." All different visions of how AI fits into society, how it relates to government, how it relates to individuals, none of them probably great, because they all presume this world in which other sources of money are not going to be here because of AI.

Leah Feiger: No, I think that's honestly a really smart way to put it, the idea of all of these companies kind of figuring out their own ways to talk about this, especially because at the end of the day, with regulatory measures and proposals changing basically hourly at this point, the government is about to go through a pretty big shift. And regardless of what happens in these elections, Trump is a lame duck president. There is a very different sense of appeal that you have to make. Are you still promising that 5 percent if you're OpenAI to a Democratic-controlled Congress? I don't know, and I'm very curious to see how that will all kind of move around. But to me, it also just gets into this larger idea of, what is the tech world's role in philanthropic movements, especially as they're shutting down their own internal CSR complaint streams as well. We've seen just over the years, over the months, so much about just the climate side of all of these companies, like I said, just being really shifted to the wayside. It's interesting, and to me, it feels like just such an obvious headline-grab as well.

Brian Barrett: Yeah. And I think to your point about the climate thing, again, going back to Anthropic, this is a company where a lot of people, not everybody, but a lot of people are at least adjacent to effective altruism, and the priorities of that set of beliefs don't necessarily line up with what you would consider to be conventional philanthropic beliefs. A lot of people, or maybe not a lot, some number of them aren't worried about climate anymore because they think AI is going to solve it. Some number of them, it's been reported, they've started smoking again because they think cancer will be a solved problem. There's a lot of assumptions about all the things that are going to be fixed. And if you are assuming that certain things are going to be fixed, you aren't going to put your public benefit money toward those things. You're going to find other places to put them no matter what the current state of urgency is on anything.

Leah Feiger: Last week, an official in the Louisiana Secretary of State's Office was going through the mail when they opened a letter and a mysterious white powder fell out. The office was evacuated. The employee was rushed to the emergency room. They were thankfully not injured, and subsequent tests showed that the substance was not harmful. By Wednesday, the office was back open and running. Bit of a scary story, going a couple of weeks into the election, but the issue here was that it wasn't a one-off. Over the course of the following days, election offices in more than 31 other states were targeted with similar letters as they prepared for the midterms. Many of those states have made public statements acknowledging the letters, but WIRED's David Gilbert, he actually is the person who broke the full extent of how far this harassment campaign went. He contacted officials in all 50 states and DC, and our accounting shows the full scale of this campaign for the very first time. It's wild. It's really, really wild. Even if this powder was not detrimental, it's very scary and clearly part of a harassment campaign for election officials leading into one of the most consequential elections in US history.

Brian Barrett: Yeah. No, the fact ... I mean, great work, David, making so many calls and putting in the work.

Leah Feiger: Truly.

Brian Barrett: So we had 32 states confirm receipt of a letter like this, and we still have a few who haven't responded yet, so the number could still go up. And, Leah, I thought it's not necessarily Democrat or Republican. It's sort of across the board, right?

Leah Feiger: Exactly. The letters also coincided with similar letters that were sent to congressional offices across the country that also targeted both Democratic and Republican lawmakers. Look, I have to say, hats off to the Postal Service. The vast majority of the letters were intercepted before they reached all of their intended targets. But in a number of states, they weren't, and election offices had to get evacuated. These offices, they're in finals mode right now. This is everything. The time that it takes to have to handle threats like this … And they're also already handling other threats. Between election denier groups and rumors of ICE at the polls, these election officials are already underwater. So the idea that there's this additional threat is just wild. The FBI and USPS say that they're investigating, but the FBI has not been clear about whether it has any leads, how many letters it's identified, anything of that nature.

Brian Barrett: Yeah. Leah, I think it's really interesting that election officials are dealing with a lot right now, and this is just one more thing to deal with. How do you see that, if at all, affecting the election? I mean, are you concerned about, not just the letters, but when you take the totality of the things that are piling up ... Again, we're two weeks out ... how concerned are you that something goes wrong or gets missed or goes awry because of the pressure on election officials making it harder to do their job than ever?

Leah Feiger: Oh my God, I mean, that's the fear. If you're listening to this podcast and you feel comfortable going out to vote, go vote. But there's a different undercurrent right now, and that's what we're hearing from NGOs, local activists, election officials, which is it's very hard to pitch the Get Out to Vote platform when there have been so many threats. All to say, right now, DHS officials have recently said they don't plan on sending immigration officers en masse to patrol the polls, but everyone's still scared because Trump has previously said in the past that that's a possibility, Republicans have previously said in the past that's a possibility. And so there's so much conflicting statements. It's very tense. It's very tense. It's something that WIRED's tracking closely. The whole WIRED politics team is very ready to keep an eye on how all of this unfolds.

Brian Barrett: Do we have any sense of the motivation of the people who are sending these white powder letters? I ask partly because on Sunday, Utah Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson posted an image of an intercepted letter to Threads. Top left-hand corner of the letter says that DSA sent it, the Democratic Socialists of America, with the New York zip code. DSA has denied any involvement. I am not saying ... To be clear, I don't think it was DSA, just to be very, very clear. But it does seem like an attempt to potentially pin it on DSA. Have we seen anything beyond Utah with that? Have we seen any other attempts to use this or leverage this, or is that just sort of an isolated thing, and really who knows?

Leah Feiger: It's so tough to say. So we haven't seen that on a larger scale, but for all that the right loves to talk about false-flag operations, this is a literal false flag, and to me is just so clearly a way to encourage ... What am I trying to say? And to me, this is clearly such a way to encourage more splits in an already very divided country. And the idea like, "Oh, no, it's the leftists. They're trying to stop the election. See, we've been calling fraud this whole time. Oh, no, it was the right," there's so many different ways to take this, and at the end of the day, it's about disunity, which is not new for American elections. I know no one likes to talk about Russian involvement or foreign involvement from elections past, but it's not ... That kind of involvement, that kind of disinformation, that kind of harassment, that rarely had to do with very specific motions like sending ICE to the polls. It had to do with encouraging people to hate each other and pretending that there was a bigger divide than there was on a variety of issues. And so I think that we're seeing this play out again, and of course we are, specifically with these letters and other examples of voter intimidation that are really concerning.

Brian Barrett: Coming up after the break, we're sharing our WIRED/TIRED picks for the week. Stay with us.

Leah Feiger: It is time for our WIRED/TIRED segment. Whatever is new and cool is wired, and whatever passé thing we're over is tired. Brian, tell me yours.

Brian Barrett: Leah, you will probably disagree with this, but only because I know you enjoy traveling to other parts of the world, you enjoy living in other parts of world. You've done it your whole life.

Leah Feiger: Sure.

Brian Barrett: But I will say TIRED is moving to another country, say, in Europe, expecting things to be dramatically better than they were in the US in some ways. I say this because we ran a great story this week from a writer named Sarah Manavis ... I hope I am pronouncing that correctly, Sarah. Apologies if not ... interviewing a bunch of expats who fled America because of Trump and found themselves ... They found that Europe was not the idyllic, countryside, perfect world that they thought it would be. Europe's great. I'm not knocking Europe. I'm not knocking moving. But it did include colorful examples such as someone who fled to Poland to avoid a far-right authoritarian government. So I guess I would say tired, more specifically would be do your research before you move to another country.

Leah Feiger: Do your research, folks. OK, what's WIRED? What's your WIRED?

Brian Barrett: Wired, I'm going to say reviewed the ... Julian Chokkattu, WIRED's gear editor, reviewed the iPhone Duo this week. The Duo is not my WIRED, but Julian's wallpaper for the Duo, which is an adorable Snoopy on a bright yellow background, it made my day. I have looked at it like 10 times today. Every time I'm feeling down, I just look at this picture of Julian's wallpaper and it makes me feel better. So I'm going to say that is WIRED.

Leah Feiger: I love that. That's pretty good. I'm going to have to go check that out. OK. My WIRED of this week is the only way that I have been avoiding election doom in 100 percent of my life is focusing on Halloween, which has been so fun. This week I am revisiting some old favorites, a.k.a. Cher's cult classic, also shout out to Susan Sarandon and Michelle Pfeiffer, The Witches of Eastwick. Highly recommend. Get some Hocus Pocus in there. There's just a lot of really, really good forms of media to revisit.

Brian Barrett: My daughter put on “This Is Halloween” from The Nightmare Before Christmas this morning before school. Really got everybody moving.

Leah Feiger: So cute. So cute. There's candy everywhere. This is helping me out right now. I'm deeply, deeply loving it. My tired is a real-life spooky tale. Our security team at wired.com has been doing an unbelievable job tracking some very serious vulnerabilities across the internet. They have a couple of big scoops, specifically the PHP Foundation revealed two serious vulnerabilities that could impact millions of websites. There's been just ... I don't know. What am I but a politics and science person? But it just feels like there has been a proliferation of very scary stories recently about vulnerabilities and hacking and the internet is no longer ours. Was it ever? So really go check out the security section so you can have a real-life Halloween experience.

Brian Barrett: And, Leah, in fairness, you're always talking about PHP.

Leah Feiger: I am always talking about PHP.

Brian Barrett: You won't shut up about it. So this is your moment in a lot of ways.

Leah Feiger: Welcome. That's our show for today. This episode was produced by Adriana Tapia.

Brian Barrett: Mixed by Pran Bandi.

Leah Feiger: Fact-checking by Matt Giles.

Brian Barrett: Our executive producer is Kate Osborn.

Leah Feiger: Our global editorial director is Katie Drummond.

entries.title: Anker Soundcore Space 2 Are at Their Lowest Price Ever
entries.summary: The Anker Soundcore Space 2 are a good deal even at full price. The fact they’re 18 percent off is just icing on the cake.
entries.content:
As WIRED’s chief headphone reviewer, I’m always asked the same question, with one follow-up. The question: What are the best headphones I should buy? The follow-up: I don’t want to spend a lot of money. My answer is also a two-parter: Always wait for a sale, or just buy Soundcore.

Soundcore is my go-to budget headphone brand. It's built a reputation as an affordable audio staple that punches far above what its price tag would suggest. Case in point: the Soundcore Space 2. They’re my current favorite over-ear headphones for anyone on a budget. They launched back in April and have gone on sale a few times, but this is the lowest price they've ever been (even lower than Prime Day).

The Best Budget Over-Ear Headphones

The Soundcore Space 2 have a lot going for them. They are understated, comfortable to wear for hours at a time, not too heavy, have easy-to-use physical button controls, and fold down nicely for stuffing into a bag.

On the inside, sound quality and active noise cancellation (ANC) are far better than you would expect for something that costs a little over $100. ANC makes everything muffled and lets me use a much more comfortable listening volume compared to other budget headphones. Battery life is killer—50 hours with ANC on, 70 hours with it off. That’s better than all the big names you usually think of (Sony, Bose, Apple) when you think of over-ear headphones.

entries.title: A New Ice Age Was Beginning. Then Humans Started Burning Fossil Fuels
entries.summary: Ancient plants reveal that the vestiges of the North American ice sheet started expanding a few thousand years ago, but that climate change caused it to reverse course.
entries.content:
Burning fossil fuels may have stopped the Earth from entering another ice age, a new study suggests. The research, published Thursday in the journal Science, uses samples of ancient vegetation and rock records to analyze the growth—and sudden retreat—of an ice cap that is the last vestige of an ice sheet that once covered much of North America.

The findings shows the Barnes Ice Cap, which covers parts of Canada’s Baffin Island, started growing a few thousand years ago before rapidly reversing course beginning in the 1960s as carbon pollution ramped up.

“A question that’s in the popular consciousness is, have we caused enough global warming to stop the next ice age from happening?” says Andrew Wickert, an associate professor of environmental science at the University of Minnesota Twin Cities, who was not involved in the research. The new research shows that “even as we were just starting to ramp up emissions, we’ve already done enough damage to cause the major North American ice sheet to already start retreating. That’s significant.”

The planet regularly goes through phases where ice extends down from the high latitudes—what we colloquially call "ice ages"—due to natural shifts in the Earth's rotation and orbit, known as Milankovitch Cycles. Those are followed by interglacial periods where ice retreats toward the poles.

The last ice age ended 12,000 years ago. At its peak, what's known as the Laurentide Ice Sheet covered all of Canada and extended as far south as New York and the Midwest. It retreated to form the Barnes Ice Cap, which covers an area the size of Delaware on Baffin Island.

Unlike glaciers, which can move, the Barnes Ice Cap is frozen to the bedrock, preserving the vegetal record of what grew around it under the ice. That quirk allowed the scientists leading the new study to glean information about how much it has grown—and shrank.

To determine when it first reached its modern size, they used an exposure dating technique to calculate roughly how long rocks several meters from the glacier’s edge had been exposed to the sky. Using measurements of Beryllium-10, an element that forms on the surface of exposed rock, the authors calculated that the ice sheet first reached the size it is today around 3,600 years ago.

Next, they wanted to see how much the ice cap had regrown from that point. To do this, they turned to the humble denizens of the tundra in front of the glacier: mosses and lichen.

“After the ice cap retreated, mosses eventually colonized this newly exposed land,” says Nicolás Young, a paleoclimatologist at the Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory at Columbia University and lead author of the new paper. “These mosses are living there, and things are normal—then, eventually, the ice cap starts to re-expand. The ice covers the moss, and kills it.” The traces of the dead moss are preserved in newly reexposed land, allowing Young and his team to piece together a timeline of how the ice has moved across the landscape.

Thanks to these records, Young and his coauthors estimate that the glacier started growing again around 2,000 years ago. This may have signaled the start of another glaciation period.

But starting in the 1960s, the ice cap has done something that wouldn’t correspond with another ice age: It started getting smaller again. The team used historic aerial photos that showed that the ice has reversed course, retreating significantly back from its new margins. The Barnes Ice Cap’s edges have retreated an average of 4 meters per year since the 1980s. That coincides with a period of rapidly increasing carbon emissions, which has caused ice to go into retreat worldwide. The ice cap offers a particularly stark example, though, given the growth prior to the 1960s.

“Modern retreat of this glacier has reversed 2,000 years of net expansion—that’s a pretty decent chunk of time,” Young says.

Meredith Kelly, a professor of earth sciences at Dartmouth, says the data gathered in the study is “awesome” and that the study shows a “clear pattern of what the ice cap was doing.” However, Kelly says that she would like to see a comparison of some of the data to other sites around the world to more fully grasp how, exactly, the Earth was moving into its glaciation period before the effects of human-caused warming kicked in. While we have a broad understanding of what kicks off periods where ice can grow, the exact mechanisms are still something that require more research.

The evidence presented in this paper, Young says, could also validate a decades-old hypothesis that has long been held up by climate deniers as “evidence” climate change is a hoax. In the early 1970s, scientists gathered for a meeting at Brown University to discuss hypotheses of when the next ice age might happen. (Young says that two of his coauthors on this paper were at that meeting.) The scientists concluded that a glaciation period was so imminent that they sent a warning letter to President Richard Nixon.

“I think this study actually helps show that scientists were right about a pending glaciation,” Young says. “

Media coverage of the meeting, as well as a colder period of weather in the 1970s, have long been pitched by climate deniers as “proof” that global warming isn’t actually happening. It very much is, though, and the new research actually adds to the evidence.

entries.title: Save $150 on the Apple Mac Mini M4, but There’s a Catch
entries.summary: Apple’s Mac Mini M4 is one of the best mini computers you can buy, and it’s $150 off. While it’s a good deal on a new, older-generation model, it’s more expensive than it was at launch.
entries.content:
Apple’s Mac Mini M4 has become a popular mini-yet-mighty desktop computer for running local agentic AI 24/7—so much so that it’s been out of stock for months. But with the introduction of the new Mac Mini M6, the older M4 is no longer as scarce (there was no M5 Mac Mini), and the base model (256-GB hard drive, 16-GB unified memory) is on sale for $649—$150 off MSRP and $250 cheaper than the M6.

It’s a good deal for a computer that is plenty powerful for most people, and some M4 Mac Mini configurations can even handle AI tasks. But—and it’s a big but—shoppers should be aware that the M4’s original base price was $599 when it launched in 2024. However, with Apple raising prices on hardware across the board this year, driven by chip and memory shortages, the M4 ended up costing $799. In comparison, the new M6 starts at $899.

Depending on how you look at it, it’s either a discount or a hard pill to swallow, knowing that it used to be much cheaper. If you’ve been eyeing a new Mac Mini and don’t need the better performance of the M6, you’re unlikely to get a lower price than this M4.

Older but Still Capable

The M4 Mac Mini may no longer be Apple’s most powerful tiny computer—that title now belongs to the M6 and M5 Pro models—but the M4 is still an incredibly strong and efficient processor. When it was discovered that it could easily run agentic AI locally, people gobbled up the Mac Mini as the affordable computing option.

Of course, for intensive tasks like AI or video editing, you really need more than 16 GB of memory; those who bought it for AI purposes loaded it up with 32 GB of RAM. For most users, however, this base-specs machine is more than capable. While the M6 system on a chip is extra powerful due to having more CPU and GPU cores, Neural Accelerators, and higher memory bandwidth, the M4 Mac Mini isn’t lagging far behind. For things like web browsing and general productivity, you won’t see much of a difference in performance.

If you need the performance, we recommend the newer M6. But for most people, the M4 Mac Mini is more than sufficient for everyday computing, and you're unlikely to find a better deal than this one.

entries.title: Fellow Aiden Precision Coffee Maker is $100 Off
entries.summary: The Fellow Aiden Precision Coffee Maker is a smart, high-end machine that offers pour-over quality. You can get it refurbished from the brand for 25 percent off.
entries.content:
The Fellow Aiden drip coffee maker is universally beloved among the WIRED Reviews team. (Read our review here.) It, alongside other popular Fellow staples, are over 20 percent off right now at Fellow's Refurbished Gear Section.

We love the Aiden partly because of its sleek, mid-century modernist design, but above all, for how easy it is to use and how great the coffee tastes. It's approachable to use but still has plenty of customization for coffee aficionados, including roast level, brewing temperature, bloom duration, and even local elevation. If you're like me and would rather press a button and go, you can choose the automated “Guided Brew” setting on the LED menu, pick your size (between five and 50 ounces), pop in a color-coded basket (which, as an added bonus, takes standard paper filters), and add the amount of coffee the drip coffee maker recommends. You'll get the perfect cup, brewed at 200 degrees Fahrenheit.

Fellow Aiden Specs

Specs
Capacity 50 ounces
Dimensions 9 x 9 x 12 inches (L x W x H)
Weight 9.6 pounds
Features Infinitely programmable, phone app, timer, cold brew, pour-over or drip settings, SCA-certified
Carafe Thermal
Warmer? No

If you're a true coffee nerd, there's the Fellow phone app where you can customize your brew and build a library of recipes to refer to later. So, if you get an exceptionally good cup of drip coffee, you can easily recreate it the next morning.

But if you're like me and would rather sip iced coffee to match your frozen heart, Aiden uses hot-bloomed coffee and a Japanese-style slow-drip method to make a light-bodied, aromatic cold brew in about 90 minutes. The brew is room temperature when it's done, so we recommend making it the night before and refrigerating it for the morning—or letting it brew a little longer and serving it over plenty of ice.

This and a few other Fellow machines and kettles are discounted as part of the brand's refurbished program (called Rebrew). Every refurbished unit the brand sells is sent to their headquarters for rigorous restoration and testing, including deep cleaning, performance testing, and component replacements. Refurbished products also come with a one-year limited warranty. Below are two other discounted Fellow electric kettles we love sitting pretty in the refurbished section.

entries.title: Meet Mori, a Cute Robot Mushroom That Doesn’t Really Say (or Do) Anything
entries.summary: Step one in convincing people to live with robots with cameras on their faces? Disguise them as cute home decor.
entries.content:
You've had a long day. You finally get home, fling the door open, plonk on the couch, and let out a big sigh. In the corner of your eye, you notice your mushroom lamp perk up. Its microphone must have heard you come in. Its head raises to reveal round, animated eyes, and a little diamond-shaped nose—which actually houses a camera.

It does a little jiggle because it sees you're back. Its name is Mori.

As you move around the space—maybe it's time to start cooking dinner—the little robot's face follows you, observing your movements and making soft sounds that are a cross between a bird and R2-D2. The day's stress catches up, and you need a moment to relax, so you head over to Mori, touch its head, and its eyes and camera-nose dip back inside its body. It goes back to being a lamp, except now it plays nature soundscapes so you can feel at ease.

That's the pitch from OKA, or One Kind Artifact, a new startup based in Cambridge, Massachusetts, and Shenzhen, China, focusing on experimental technology. CEO Hua Wang tells WIRED he wants his company to create five experimental “Artifacts” over the course of OKA's lifetime. Mori is the first.

“There are certain relationships in this era we want to fix between humans and our surroundings—human with nature, human with one another—every product is an experience trying to reconnect some of those relationships,” Wang says. Before cofounding OKA, he was a general manager at Meipai, a video-sharing app from the Chinese phone brand Meitu. He also cofounded Bondee, a now-defunct social media app that briefly went viral in Asia.

According to the company, the point of Mori, the nearly 12-inch-tall home robot lamp, is to reconnect its owners with nature. It can play nature soundscapes. It will glow different colors—inspired by rain, forests, fire, and wind—while reacting to your movements. It can guide you through a calming breathing session.

It also uses its built-in camera and microphones to serve as a fun little interactive companion in your home. Ask it how your outfit looks, and Mori will jiggle excitedly. If you're playing music or watching TV, Mori can dance to the tunes and react to the action on your TV screen.

It intentionally does not do anything else. Unlike an Amazon Echo, it isn't an assistant: You can't use voice commands to control smart lights or cue up Spotify tracks, and it won't answer if you ask about the weather.

The Founder's Edition is a staggering $649 and is available starting today, though stock is limited to a few hundred units. That price also includes a two-year warranty and two years of Mori's subscription service ($17 per month or $80 a year). If you miss out on the Founder’s Edition, you can still buy a standard edition Mori, but that costs $849 (there's a preorder price of $799), and that higher price shockingly does not include any of the subscription features.

The breathing exercises are free, and you can still access those without a subscription. But if you want the nature soundscapes, you need to subscribe. Otherwise, Mori is just a glorified lamp that dances a little bit while pointing its camera at you and any other people in your home.

Wang says today's home robots have mostly taken on “machine-like” forms that don't mesh well with personal environments, so OKA designed a lamp that blends in, but is also anthropomorphized to make being at home “feel better.”

OKA's AI algorithms (powered by multiple local large language models) let Mori understand the room's context through the camera and microphone, so it knows when to interact and when to stay quiet. The company calls this “Attentive Intelligence.” It has memory, so it remembers you and interacts with you a certain way over time, whereas it might act a little more shy if you bring home a guest. If it doesn't see someone for a month, it will forget them.

It might notice, for example, that you've been on your phone doomscrolling for two hours straight on the couch. Mori might then try to get your attention so you come over, listen to some wind rustling through the leaves, and give your eyes a break. When you're on a phone call, or maybe having an argument with a significant other, it understands what’s happening and goes silent so as not to distract you.

“All gadgets try to capture more of your attention,” Wang says. “Mori gives your attention back to you. It invites you to do meditative experiences. Nature has this restorative power to humans.”

The robot can connect to Wi-Fi, which should give you pause from a security standpoint, but Wang says the internet connection is only used for firmware updates.

Mori processes raw images and audio locally, and then discards the files. Facial feature data—which is collected so it knows to react to you versus a guest—is encrypted on the device, and never uploaded. The camera turns off when the robot retracts into a lamp, and the microphone turns off when you double-tap the top of Mori's head. It is battery-powered, so you can take it from room to room, or just leave it plugged in.

Wang says Mori's skill set is limited for now, though it could expand in the future. He suggests it could connect to your Oura Ring data in the future so it knows exactly when you need some relaxing sounds, or to your Spotify account to play different content. Voice commands could even come later—like asking Mori to play nature sounds instead of having to touch it.

“People feel isolated and want this kind of presence in their home. A lot of people leave their TV on to fill the emptiness of the room,” Wang says, pointing to a time when he was feeling isolated while studying abroad in the US. “It's not particularly for the elderly or children, but for younger generations.”

Cute robot pets that interact with you have been welcomed into our homes before. Chris Harrison, director of the Future Interfaces Group at Carnegie Mellon University, points to Sony's Aibo dog from 1999 as an early digital companion. However, he says the crucial ingredient they have been missing is what artificial intelligence can now provide. These previous robots were too simplistic, but now that the modern versions can understand and react to human actions and emotions, they could become more impactful.

“Humans have always wanted to anthropomorphize everything—they love making things cute,” Harrison says. “We want to make robots cute; we want to put cute little cases on our iPhones.” He points to Meta's new Muse agent, which has a cuddly avatar. “It is almost like a pet, but a hyper-capable pet.”

When I point out that Mori doesn't seem very capable with its limited feature set, Harrison likens it to people owning a goldfish or a hamster.

“Are we holding [Mori] to an unrealistic bar? People do extract a lot of pleasure out of taking care of their pets and snuggling with their pets and interacting with their pets that I wouldn't say are necessarily more sophisticated.”

Whether people will shell out hundreds of dollars for a robotic pet that can’t fetch—or even tell you the time—is up in the air. But if this mushroom-shaped, camera-wielding lamp can fool overstimulated brains into feeling a little less alone at the end of the day, maybe that’s enough.
